docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Cloud Native GIS is a platform for handling layers and served on map.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
Layer can be in vector and raster and being served as tile.

Style is saved in database. Vector layer is in mapbox style.

Maputnik is being used to change the style.

docs.title: Production
docs.text:
git submodule update
git clone https://github.com/kartoza/CloudNativeGIS
cp deployment/.template.env deployment/.env
cp deployment/docker-compose.override.template deployment/docker-compose.template
make up

The web will be available at http://127.0.0.1/

To stop containers:

make kill

To stop and delete containers:

make down

docs.title: Install as django library
docs.text:
This application can be installed as django library.

To install it, put git+https://github.com/kartoza/CloudNativeGIS.git to requirements. Add cloud_native_gis to INSTALLED_APPS, and add url path('', include('cloud_native_gis.urls')).

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
git submodule update
git clone https://github.com/kartoza/CloudNativeGIS
cp deployment/.template.env deployment/.env
cp deployment/docker-compose.override.template deployment/docker-compose.template

After that, do

  • open new terminal
  • on folder root of project, do
make serve

Wait until it is done when there is sentence "webpack xxx compiled successfully in xxx ms". After that, don't close the terminal. If it is accidentally closed, do make serve again

Next step:

  • Open new terminal
  • Do commands below
make up
make dev

Wait until it is on.

The web can be accessed using http://localhost:5000/

If the web is taking long time to load, restart cloud_native_gis_dev_1 container. The sequence should be make dev, after that run or restart cloud_native_gis_dev_1.

docs.title: Maputnik updates
docs.text:
CloudNativeGIS using maputnik to edit style. We could update maputnik in the folder root/maputnik. Maputnik can be accessed in the django-admin and layers, and there is "editor" column that will be redirect to maputnik instance. By default, it is using maputnik production.

To change and test maputnik:

make serve-maputnik

After it is done, there will be link to maputnik. Copy the link and paste in: go to deployment/.env change MAPUTNIK_URL to the copied link

restart dev container

After done, we need to update the maputnik production. First, create commit of maputnik and push it to repo. Then

make build-maputnik

It will create files in the django_project/cloud_native_gis/templates/maputnik.html and also assets in the django_project/cloud_native_gis/static

After that, test it by remove MAPUTNIK_URL and restart dev container. If satisfied, just create commit for the changes.

docs.title: Administrator Guide
docs.text: This guide covers the installation, configuration, and maintenance of Cloud Native GIS.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Cloud Native GIS is a Django-based platform that can be deployed as:

  • A standalone application using Docker
  • A Django library integrated into existing projects

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
• Deployment - Installation and deployment options
  • Configuration - Environment variables and settings
  • Maintenance - Backup, monitoring, and troubleshooting

docs.title: Minimum Requirements
docs.text: Component Requirement CPU 2 cores RAM 4 GB Storage 20 GB SSD OS Linux (Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 11+)

docs.title: Recommended Requirements
docs.text: Component Requirement CPU 4+ cores RAM 8+ GB Storage 100+ GB SSD OS Linux with Docker

docs.title: Software Dependencies
docs.text:
• Python: 3.10, 3.11, or 3.12
  • PostgreSQL: 13+ with PostGIS 3.0+
  • Docker: 20.10+ (for containerized deployment)
  • Node.js: 18+ (for frontend development)

docs.title: Docker Deployment
docs.text:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/kartoza/CloudNativeGIS
cd CloudNativeGIS

# Configure environment
cp deployment/.template.env deployment/.env
cp deployment/docker-compose.override.template deployment/docker-compose.override.yml

# Edit .env with your settings
nano deployment/.env

# Start the application
make up

docs.text:
pip install cloud-native-gis

Add to your Django settings:

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    # ...
    'cloud_native_gis',
    # ...
]

Add to your URLs:

urlpatterns = [
    # ...
    path('', include('cloud_native_gis.urls')),
]

docs.title: Consuming a converted layer
docs.text: CloudBench converts files already sitting in a bucket into web-ready layers, in the background (see CloudBench S3 conversion process for how that conversion itself runs). This page is for whoever consumes the result - a map developer, a data analyst, an AI agent exploring the bucket - not for maintaining CloudBench itself.

docs.title: What you get, and where
docs.text:
Each converted layer lands in its own folder of the bucket, laid out as a Portolan "single-file collection" - the same shape whether it came from a vector source or a raster one:

File For collection.json The layer's metadata: license, bounding box, and its assets - see below. The thing to fetch first; everything else is linked from it. README.md A human reading the bucket directly (e.g. browsing it in a file manager). AGENTS.md An AI agent exploring the bucket: which asset to actually query, and which are just for rendering. styles/default.json A ready-to-use MapLibre style - point a map straight at it, no styling work needed.

Within collection.json, each asset is tagged with a role that tells you which file to use for what - this is the main thing worth knowing, since every layer produces more than one file and they are not interchangeable:

  • data - the file to query or analyse (a GeoParquet for vector, the original-CRS COG for raster). Never the one to put on a map directly.
  • visual - the file a map renders (PMTiles for vector, the EPSG:3857 COG for raster).
  • thumbnail - a small PNG preview.
  • source (GeoPackage only) - the original upload, kept alongside its converted layers.

A GeoPackage's several layers are grouped under one sub-catalog folder (a shared catalog.json linking each layer's own collection.json) rather than scattered at the top level, so discovering the bucket shows them as one dataset, not loose files.

docs.title: Vector layers: PMTiles (render) + GeoParquet (query)
docs.text:
Both files are static - there is no tile server or query API behind them, only the bucket (or a CDN in front of it):

  • PMTiles packs every zoom/tile into one file with its own internal index, so a map library (pmtiles / maplibre-gl / leaflet) fetches exactly the tile(s) it needs with plain HTTP range requests - no backend to run, and nothing to pre-warm.
  • GeoParquet's bbox-covering column and row-group layout let a reader (duckdb, geopandas, pyarrow) skip straight to the row groups that overlap an area of interest, without downloading the whole file or needing a spatial database - a plain duckdb query against the object's URL (via its httpfs/spatial extensions) can filter spatially before a single row is parsed.

Querying the PMTiles for individual feature attributes isn't the intended use - tiles are simplified per zoom level, and features can be split across tile boundaries. Use the GeoParquet for that; use the PMTiles only to render.

docs.title: Raster layers: two COGs, for two different jobs
docs.text:
A COG is a regular GeoTIFF with its internal tiles and overviews laid out so a client can read just the part it needs over plain HTTP (GDAL's /vsicurl/, rasterio, rio-tiler, titiler, QGIS's "Add Layer from URL", ...) - never the whole file, even for a single pixel value or a zoomed-out overview.

Pick the variant for what you're doing with it, not by habit - don't download and reproject the one you grabbed instead of fetching the right one:

  • The original-CRS COG (data asset) for anything that measures or analyses the raster (area, zonal statistics, sampling) - reprojecting first would distort those measurements.
  • The _3857 COG (visual asset) for a web map - most map libraries (MapLibre/Leaflet/OpenLayers) render in Web Mercator, and maplibre-cog-protocol specifically only accepts this one.

Both carry their band statistics (min/max/mean/stddev) embedded in the file's own header, so a client can colour-stretch the raster sensibly straight from that - no full-raster scan needed just to render it reasonably.

docs.title: A bulk upload's VRT
docs.text:
A bulk upload may also publish one GDAL VRT ("virtual raster") over all the GeoTIFFs it converted that share a CRS, band count and data type - letting you open one file and see the whole compatible set as a single continuous dataset, instead of requesting and mosaicking each COG yourself.

A few things worth knowing before you reach for it:

  • It's metadata only - an XML file referencing the underlying COGs, not a re-encoded copy. Opening it still reads pixels from the original COGs over HTTP; nothing is pre-rendered.
  • It's linked from the bucket's root catalog (so it's discoverable), but it has no renderable asset of its own - open it with desktop GIS or GDAL tooling (gdalinfo, QGIS, rasterio), not CloudBench's own Map Explorer.
  • Not every raster in the batch is necessarily covered - one with a different CRS, band count or data type is left out of the VRT (and told why), though it's still published as its own ordinary COG collection regardless.

docs.title: Deployment Guide
docs.text: This guide covers various deployment options for Cloud Native GIS.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker 20.10+
  • Docker Compose 2.0+
  • Git

docs.title: Step-by-Step Installation
docs.text:
# 1. Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/kartoza/CloudNativeGIS
cd CloudNativeGIS

# 2. Initialize submodules
git submodule update --init --recursive

# 3. Copy configuration templates
cp deployment/.template.env deployment/.env
cp deployment/docker-compose.override.template deployment/docker-compose.override.yml

# 4. Edit environment variables
nano deployment/.env

# 5. Start the application
make up

docs.text: Service Description Port nginx Reverse proxy 80 django Application server 5000 db PostgreSQL/PostGIS 5432 dev Development server 5000

docs.title: Verifying Installation
docs.text:
1. Open http://localhost/ in your browser
  2. Access admin at http://localhost/admin/
  3. Default credentials are in your .env file

docs.title: Using Docker Compose
docs.text:
# docker-compose.prod.yml
version: '3.8'

services:
  nginx:
    image: kartoza/cloud_native_gis:latest
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - ./ssl:/etc/nginx/ssl:ro
    depends_on:
      - django

  django:
    image: kartoza/cloud_native_gis:latest
    restart: always
    env_file:
      - .env.prod
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: kartoza/postgis:15-3.3
    restart: always
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    env_file:
      - .env.prod

volumes:
  pgdata:

docs.title: Using Docker

gzip backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).sql

# /etc/cron.d/cloudnativegis-backup
0 2 * * * root docker compose -f /path/to/docker-compose.yml exec -T db pg_dump -U postgres cloudnativegis | gzip > /backups/db_$(date +\%Y\%m\%d).sql.gz

gunzip -c backup_20240101.sql.gz | docker compose exec -T db psql -U postgres cloudnativegis

docs.title: For Developers
docs.text: This is the homepage for all developer related documentation.

docs.title: CloudBench S3 conversion process
docs.text:
CloudBench (kartoza-cloudbench) converts files already sitting in an S3-compatible bucket into web-ready layers, in the background: a user uploads nothing through their browser, and may convert one file at a time or a whole folder at once ("bulk upload"). This page documents how that background conversion actually runs - the commands and arguments involved - split into the two format families CloudBench converts, plus the VRT CloudBench can build afterwards over a bulk upload's rasters.

Two separate codebases are involved:

  • CloudNativeGIS Processing ("cng-node") - a small, database-free FastAPI service that does the actual conversion: it downloads (or reads from the same bucket) the source file, runs the GDAL/tippecanoe commands below, and uploads every result straight to the destination bucket itself, via a presigned URL per file.
  • CloudBench - submits the conversion job to cng-node (one running on a fixed server, or one on-demand, per job, started on Hetzner Cloud), polls it to completion, and writes the Portolan catalog metadata once it's done. For a bulk upload, it also optionally builds a VRT of the batch's GeoTIFFs itself, directly with GDAL - no cng-node job for that.
flowchart TD
    CB["CloudBench"]
    CNG["CloudNativeGIS Processing (cng-node)<br/>runs GDAL / tippecanoe"]
    S3[("S3-compatible bucket")]

    CB -->|"1. submit job"| CNG
    CNG -->|"2. read the source"| S3
    CNG -->|"3. upload each result"| S3
    CB -->|"4. poll until done"| CNG
    CB -->|"5. write Portolan<br/>catalog metadata"| S3

docs.title: Tool versions
docs.text:
cng-node's image (processing/Dockerfile) pins these:

Tool Version Source GDAL (gdal_translate, gdalwarp, gdalinfo, ogr2ogr, ogrmerge.py) 3.11.4 ghcr.io/osgeo/gdal:ubuntu-full-3.11.4 - the "full" build, needed for Arrow/(Geo)Parquet support tippecanoe unpinned - whatever's on main when the image is built felt/tippecanoe, not the original mapbox/tippecanoe - built from source, git clone --depth 1 PDAL (LAS/LAZ → COPC; not covered on this page) 2.10 conda-forge

Nothing above a few hundred MB is ever downloaded to CloudBench's own disk: cng-node reads the source and writes every result through presigned URLs, and the VRT step below only ever reads a COG's header, not its pixels.

This page is about how the conversion itself runs. For what the files it produces actually are and how to use them, see Consuming a converted layer.

docs.title: Vector layers → PMTiles + GeoParquet
docs.text:
A shapefile (as a .zip), GeoPackage, GeoJSON, FlatGeobuf or KML/KMZ becomes a pair of files per layer: a GeoParquet (the analysis-ready data, in the source's own CRS) and a PMTiles (the web-map rendering) - the pairing the Portolan spec asks for.

flowchart LR
    A[Source] --> B["1. Normalise<br/>(KML/KMZ only)"]
    B --> C["2. Export for tiling"]
    B --> D["4. Write GeoParquet"]
    C --> E["3. tippecanoe<br/>→ PMTiles"]

Steps 2+3 and step 4 both only read the (normalised) source, so they run at the same time, not one after the other - see step 4 below.

docs.title: 1. Normalise to one layer
docs.text:
A KML/KMZ with several <Folder>s is merged into one GeoPackage layer first (LIBKML reads each folder as its own OGR layer, but GeoParquet holds exactly one), keeping each feature's folder name in a folder column:

ogrmerge.py -single -f GPKG -o merged.gpkg \
  -nln merged \
  -lco GEOMETRY_NAME=geometry \
  -src_layer_field_name folder \
  -src_layer_field_content "{LAYER_NAME}" \
  <source>

A GeoPackage's own layers, and any other single-layer source, skip this step.

docs.title: 2. Export features for tiling
docs.text:
The layer is exported as line-delimited GeoJSON (GeoJSONSeq), reprojected to WGS84 - the CRS tippecanoe tiles in:

ogr2ogr -f GeoJSONSeq [-s_srs EPSG:4326] -t_srs EPSG:4326 <output>.geojsonl <source> [<layer>]

-s_srs EPSG:4326 is only added when the source has no coordinate system of its own (e.g. a shapefile missing its .prj) - rather than failing the conversion, WGS84 is assumed, since that's the common case.

docs.title: 3. Tile with tippecanoe to create the PMTiles
docs.text:
tippecanoe --force -P --projection=EPSG:4326 \
  --smallest-maximum-zoom-guess=<floor> \
  --no-simplification-of-shared-nodes \
  -o <output>.pmtiles -l <layer-name> <input>.geojsonl
Flag Why -P Reads the GeoJSONSeq input in parallel. --smallest-maximum-zoom-guess=<floor> tippecanoe's own -zg guesses a layer's max zoom from the typical spacing between features - a layer with both dense and sparse areas (e.g. a country's neighbourhoods: packed in cities, sparse elsewhere) can get dragged down to a low guess by its sparser areas, blowing up blocky tiles client-side exactly at the zoom someone's actually looking at. --smallest-maximum-zoom-guess is -zg's own density-based guess with a floor: unlike plain -zg it never refuses to guess, so there's no separate fallback to handle. It never lowers a denser layer's own higher guess. The floor is DEFAULT_MIN_MEANINGFUL_ZOOM (9) unless the API request names a different min_meaningful_zoom. --no-simplification-of-shared-nodes Simplifies an edge shared between adjacent polygons (e.g. neighbouring admin boundaries) the same way on both sides, so low zoom doesn't show a gap or sliver along the shared border.

tippecanoe's own stderr progress (Maxzoom: NN%, then z/x/y NN.N%) is parsed live and relayed to CloudBench's polling as the job's progress message.

A timeout scales with input size - 300s base, +20min per GB, capped at 3h - so a genuinely large layer gets the time it needs (2.8M buildings, 1.1GB, take ~3 minutes on 16 cores) while a pathological geometry (e.g. a near-global polygon forced to a high zoom) can't run away forever.

docs.title: 4. Write the GeoParquet
docs.text:
Run alongside tippecanoe (both only read the source), not after it:

ogr2ogr -f Parquet \
  -lco COMPRESSION=ZSTD -lco WRITE_COVERING_BBOX=YES -lco ROW_GROUP_SIZE=100000 \
  [-a_srs EPSG:4326] \
  <output>.parquet <source> [<layer>]

This satisfies Portolan's GeoParquet requirements: GeoParquet 1.1, with a per-row-group bbox-covering column, row groups capped at 150k rows (100,000 is used), and zstd compression. The rows are then re-ordered along a spatial curve (not GDAL's own SORT_BY_BBOX, which doesn't pack them tightly enough for Portolan).

docs.title: Raster (TIFF, or a GeoPackage's raster tables) → COG
docs.text:
A GeoTIFF, or a raster table inside a GeoPackage, becomes two Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs: the original-CRS one, and an EPSG:3857 (Web Mercator) one.

The second variant exists purely for rendering. MapLibre's map canvas is Web Mercator throughout, and maplibre-cog-protocol (the library Map Explorer uses to add a COG as a map source) reads windows of the COG straight into MapLibre's WebGL pipeline with no reprojection step - too slow to do per frame in the browser - so the COG itself has to already be in EPSG:3857. That reprojection happens once, up front, via gdalwarp below, instead of on every pan or zoom. The original-CRS COG is kept alongside it for anything that measures the raster (see Consuming a converted layer) - reprojecting first would distort that.

gdal_translate -of COG -co COMPRESS=DEFLATE -co BLOCKSIZE=512 -co STATISTICS=YES \
  <input>.tif <output>.tif

gdalwarp -t_srs EPSG:3857 -of COG -co COMPRESS=DEFLATE -co BLOCKSIZE=512 -co STATISTICS=YES \
  <input>.tif <output>_3857.tif

Both variants go through the same COG_OPTIONS. After each, gdalinfo -json (with GDAL_PAM_ENABLED=NO, so it can't fall back to a sidecar .aux.xml) checks every band actually carries its min/max/mean/stddev embedded in the file itself - if any are missing, the conversion fails rather than publishing a COG a client would have to compute statistics for itself. (Needs a GDAL build with STATISTICS=YES support for the COG driver - GDAL ≥ 3.8.)

docs.title: Building a VRT (bulk upload only)
docs.text: A bulk upload may also publish a GDAL VRT ("virtual raster") of its GeoTIFFs, once every layer's COG conversion is done - a single mosaic-like overview over the whole batch's rasters, without re-encoding any pixel. This step runs in CloudBench itself, not in cng-node - see apps/s3/bulk_vrt.py.

docs.title: 1. Read each COG's header only
docs.text:
Rather than downloading every COG in full, only the start of each file is fetched - enough for GDAL to read its header (its CRS, band count, data type, extent), not its pixel data - via an HTTP range request against the bucket:

GET <cog-key>  Range: bytes=0-1048575

If gdalinfo can't parse that much (a very large raster's tile-offset arrays can run long), it's retried with a bigger range - 16 MiB, then 256 MiB - stopping once a read comes back shorter than asked for (the whole file, however small).

docs.title: 2. Group rasters that can share one VRT
docs.text: Not every raster in a batch can go in the same VRT: a VRT's members must share a CRS, band count and data type (not nodata - each source keeps its own in a VRT, unlike a true mosaic's tiles). The largest such group is kept; anything that doesn't match it is left out of the VRT, each with why (e.g. "in EPSG:3857, not EPSG:32735", "2 band(s), not 1") - but every layer, in or out, is still published as its own COG collection regardless.

docs.title: 3. Build the VRT
docs.text:
gdalbuildvrt -resolution highest <name>.vrt <relative-path-to-each-cog>...

Run with the batch's common parent folder as its working directory, and each COG given as a path relative to that folder - /vsicurl/ (reading straight from a URL) doesn't resolve a ../ the way a local path would, so every path in the VRT must run down from where the VRT itself sits, never up and back down.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Consuming a converted layer - what the files these conversions produce actually are, and how to use each one.
  • apps/s3/cng_lite.py in kartoza-cloudbench - how a job's steps (provision, push, poll, verify, publish) are driven from the CloudBench side.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: Welcome to the Cloud Native GIS User Guide. This section provides comprehensive documentation for end users working with the platform.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
New to Cloud Native GIS? Start here:

  • Getting Started - Your first steps with Cloud Native GIS
  • Working with Layers - Understanding and managing geospatial layers
  • Styling Your Maps - Using Maputnik to create beautiful map styles

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Cloud Native GIS supports both vector and raster layers, served as tiles for efficient map rendering.

  • Vector Layers: Point, line, and polygon data stored in PostGIS and served as vector tiles
  • Raster Layers: Image data served as Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs (COG) or PMTiles

docs.title: Styles
docs.text:
Map styles are stored in the database using the Mapbox Style Specification. This allows for:

  • Consistent styling across all map views
  • Version control of style changes
  • Easy sharing of styles between layers

docs.title: Maputnik Integration
docs.text:
Maputnik is the built-in style editor that allows you to:

  • Visually design map styles
  • Preview changes in real-time
  • Export styles in standard Mapbox GL format

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide will help you get started with Cloud Native GIS, from your first login to creating your first map layer.

docs.title: Accessing the Platform
docs.text:
After installation, access Cloud Native GIS through your web browser:

  • Production: http://your-domain.com/
  • Development: http://localhost:5000/

docs.title: Django Admin Interface
docs.text:
Cloud Native GIS uses Django's admin interface for layer and style management. Access it at:

http://your-domain.com/admin/

docs.title: Logging In
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the admin URL
  2. Enter your username and password
  3. Click "Log in"

Note

Contact your administrator if you don't have credentials.

docs.title: Step 1: Prepare Your Data
docs.text:
Cloud Native GIS supports various geospatial formats:

  • Shapefiles (.shp with accompanying files)
  • GeoJSON (.geojson, .json)
  • GeoPackage (.gpkg)
  • KML (.kml)

docs.title: Step 2: Upload the Layer
docs.text:
1. Go to Cloud Native GIS > Layers in the admin
  2. Click Add Layer
  3. Fill in the layer details:
  4. Name: A descriptive name for your layer
  5. Description: Optional description
  6. File: Upload your geospatial file
  7. Click Save

docs.title: Step 3: Configure the Layer
docs.text:
After upload, the layer will be processed and you can:

  • View the layer attributes
  • Set the default style
  • Configure tile serving options

docs.title: Viewing Your Layer
docs.text:
Once a layer is created, you can:

  1. Preview in Admin: Click on the layer to see a map preview
  2. Access via API: Use the REST API to fetch layer data
  3. Embed in Applications: Use the tile URLs in your mapping application

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Working with Layers - Deep dive into layer management
  • Styling Your Maps - Learn to style your layers
  • API Reference - Integrate with your applications

docs.title: Working with Layers
docs.text: Layers are the fundamental building blocks of Cloud Native GIS. This guide covers everything you need to know about creating, managing, and serving geospatial layers.

docs.title: Vector Layers
docs.text:
Vector layers contain geometric features (points, lines, polygons) with associated attributes.

Supported formats:

  • Shapefile (.shp)
  • GeoJSON (.geojson)
  • GeoPackage (.gpkg)
  • KML (.kml)
  • CSV with geometry (.csv)

Storage: Vector data is stored in PostGIS and served as Mapbox Vector Tiles (MVT).

docs.title: Raster Layers
docs.text:
Raster layers contain gridded data such as satellite imagery, elevation models, or thematic maps.

Supported formats:

  • GeoTIFF (.tif, .tiff)
  • Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (COG)
  • PMTiles (.pmtiles)

docs.title: Creating a Layer
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Upload File] --> B[Process Data]
    B --> C[Store in PostGIS]
    C --> D[Generate Tiles]
    D --> E[Apply Style]
  1. Navigate to Admin > Cloud Native GIS > Layers
  2. Click Add Layer
  3. Fill in the required fields:
  4. Name: Unique identifier for the layer
  5. Title: Display name
  6. Description: Layer description
  7. File: Your geospatial data file

docs.title: Layer Properties
docs.text: Property Description name Unique layer identifier title Human-readable display name description Layer description created_at Creation timestamp updated_at Last modification timestamp bbox Bounding box (auto-calculated) srid Spatial Reference ID

docs.title: Updating a Layer
docs.text:
To update layer data:

  1. Go to the layer in admin
  2. Upload a new file
  3. The old data will be replaced

Warning

Updating a layer replaces all existing features. Consider creating a new layer version instead.

docs.title: Deleting a Layer
docs.text:
1. Select the layer(s) in the admin list
  2. Choose "Delete selected layers" from the action dropdown
  3. Confirm deletion

Danger

Layer deletion is permanent and cannot be undone.

docs.title: Vector Tiles (MVT)
docs.text:
Vector layers are served as Mapbox Vector Tiles:

/api/v1/layer/{layer_id}/tile/{z}/{x}/{y}.mvt

docs.title: Raster Tiles
docs.text:
Raster layers support multiple formats:

# PNG tiles
/api/v1/layer/{layer_id}/tile/{z}/{x}/{y}.png

# JPEG tiles
/api/v1/layer/{layer_id}/tile/{z}/{x}/{y}.jpg

docs.title: PMTiles
docs.text:
For PMTiles layers, use the direct PMTile endpoint:

/api/v1/pmtile/{layer_id}/{path}

docs.title: Viewing Attributes
docs.text:
Each vector layer has associated attributes that can be:

  • Viewed in the admin interface
  • Queried via the API
  • Used for styling rules

docs.title: Attribute Types
docs.text: Type Description string Text values integer Whole numbers float Decimal numbers boolean True/False values date Date values datetime Date and time values

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use descriptive names: Choose clear, meaningful layer names
  2. Optimize data: Simplify geometries for web display
  3. Set appropriate zoom levels: Configure min/max zoom for performance
  4. Apply styles: Create styles to enhance visualization
  5. Document layers: Add descriptions and metadata

Made with by Kartoza | Donate! | GitHub

docs.title: Styling Your Maps
docs.text: Cloud Native GIS uses the Mapbox Style Specification for styling layers. The built-in Maputnik editor provides a visual interface for creating and editing styles.

docs.title: Understanding Map Styles
docs.text:
A map style defines how layers are rendered, including:

  • Colors: Fill, stroke, and text colors
  • Sizes: Line widths, symbol sizes
  • Typography: Font families, sizes, and placement
  • Filters: Data-driven styling rules
  • Zoom levels: Scale-dependent rendering

docs.title: Accessing Maputnik
docs.text:
1. Go to Admin > Cloud Native GIS > Layers
  2. Click on a layer
  3. Click the Editor link in the layer detail view

docs.title: Creating a Style
docs.text:
1. Select a layer from the sources panel
  2. Add a style layer for the data source
  3. Configure properties:
  4. Paint properties (visual appearance)
  5. Layout properties (positioning)
  6. Filter expressions (data selection)
  7. Preview your changes in real-time
  8. Save the style

docs.title: Fill Layers (Polygons)
docs.text:
{
  "fill-color": "#3388ff",
  "fill-opacity": 0.6,
  "fill-outline-color": "#000000"
}

docs.title: Line Layers
docs.text:
{
  "line-color": "#ff0000",
  "line-width": 2,
  "line-opacity": 1,
  "line-dasharray": [2, 4]
}

docs.title: Symbol Layers (Points/Labels)
docs.text:
{
  "icon-image": "marker",
  "icon-size": 1.5,
  "text-field": ["get", "name"],
  "text-size": 12,
  "text-color": "#333333"
}

docs.title: Data-Driven Styling
docs.text: Use expressions to style features based on their attributes:

docs.title: Color by Category
docs.text:
{
  "fill-color": [
    "match",
    ["get", "type"],
    "residential", "#ffcc00",
    "commercial", "#0066ff",
    "industrial", "#ff6600",
    "#cccccc"
  ]
}

docs.title: Size by Value
docs.text:
{
  "circle-radius": [
    "interpolate",
    ["linear"],
    ["get", "population"],
    0, 5,
    100000, 20,
    1000000, 40
  ]
}

docs.title: Zoom-Dependent Styling
docs.text:
{
  "line-width": [
    "interpolate",
    ["linear"],
    ["zoom"],
    10, 1,
    15, 4,
    20, 8
  ]
}

docs.title: Style Storage
docs.text:
Styles are stored in the database and linked to layers. Each layer can have:

  • One default style
  • Multiple named style variants

docs.title: Exporting Styles
docs.text:
1. Open the layer in Maputnik
  2. Click Export in the menu
  3. Download as JSON

docs.title: Importing Styles
docs.text:
1. Open the layer in Maputnik
  2. Click Import
  3. Upload your JSON style file

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Start simple: Begin with basic colors, then add complexity
  2. Use zoom levels: Adjust detail based on zoom
  3. Consider accessibility: Use color-blind friendly palettes
  4. Test on different devices: Ensure styles work across screens
  5. Document your styles: Add comments and descriptions
